summary:
The Pitcairn Islands are a British Overseas Territory. Defence and external affairs are reserved to the United Kingdom, and United Kingdom domestic measures do not extend to Pitcairn of their own force; local ordinance governs.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001, so a visitor faces no criminalisation exposure on that ground.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, in force since 2010. The guarantee is constitutional rather than an offence provision, and it names sexual orientation and not gender identity, so a trans visitor has no express constitutional protection on gender-identity grounds.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, so the local definition of marriage carries no birth-sex or gender-identity bar.

The same ordinance recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn, which supports recognition of a visitor's existing foreign partnership.

The permanent population is roughly 50 and no resident is known to be in a same-sex relationship. There is no documented trans or LGB community presence, and a visitor cannot be anonymous in a population that small.

No trans-specific violence has been reported in the Pitcairn Islands, and no sourced reporting documents hostility toward visitors on these grounds.
tangentialFactors:
The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 was approved unanimously by the Island Council on 1 April 2015, signed by Governor Jonathan Sinclair on 5 May 2015, and published on 13 May 2015.

Military service is a United Kingdom responsibility rather than a local one.
localsOnly:
Adoption has been legal since 2015 and is open to married, unmarried and single people.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 is the standing local non-discrimination instrument for residents. It covers sexual orientation only and does not name gender identity, so a trans resident has no express constitutional ground of complaint.
outOfScopeNotes:
The three sources consulted are mirrors of a single encyclopaedia article. No primary legislative text or government source was consulted, so the ordinance's exact wording on gender identity is not independently verified.

No sourced information was identified on how Pitcairn authorities handle identity documents or gender markers for visitors, or on entry and screening practice.

No sourced information was identified on trans-specific healthcare or facilities on the island.

No local provision on single-sex services or facilities was identified in the sources.

No sourced record was identified of how the constitutional non-discrimination guarantee has been applied or enforced.
